utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I should remind you, the affirmation you made to tell the truth still --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will repeat so that I'm on air. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Ms. Kravetz continues her questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit P1098 up on the screen and I would like page 13 of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday when we left off we were speaking about your report on the Kosovo Cultural Heritage Project, and I would like you to comment on a page of your report which will soon be up on the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have only the English displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the results of our survey projected onto a map. The different-coloured dots represent monuments that had been damaged or destroyed. The different colours pertain to the category of architecture that we're talking about. Yellow is historic civil architecture, red is architecture of the Islamic heritage in Kosovo, blue is Catholic architecture, and purple is Orthodox architecture, Serbian Orthodox. And the size of the dot represents the number of sites at any given location that were destroyed or damaged. As you can see, it's a small territory and the damage was quite pervasive. It wasn't isolated to a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that this map has the date below in the legend of March 1998 to October 1999. I understand that's the period that's covered by your report. In your report you indicate - and I believe this is on page 8 --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a copy with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's okay. That -- you give the number of mosques destroyed and you say that that is approximately 225 in total. Now, is this number for the entire period of March 1998 to 1999 or does it cover a specific period?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It covers the entire period of the survey of the -- that we covered for the survey, so damage that occurred from the first spring and summer of the armed conflict until June of 1999. And then continuing through the time of our survey, which was October of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And yesterday you told us about how you went about conducting this survey. How were you able to establish whether damage to the mosques that you considered for this survey was done in 1998 or in 1999, how did you obtain that information?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a number of sources of information. The primary source of course was the affected community, the various churches or the Islamic Community, who almost invariably stated when their monuments were damaged or destroyed. However, we tried, whenever possible, to confirm that kind of information through informant statements, if any informants came forward, if they had seen it. Secondly, media accounts, for example, during the first summer of the war, in the summer of 1998, there were a number of journalists in Kosovo, many more than stayed during the spring of 1999. And in their reports they would observe that in a certain village a mosque was damaged or similar kind of damage. And so that allowed us to confirm dates and establish them that day. Whenever possible, we always tried to corroborate information from multiple independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could very briefly go back to the map on page 13, I wanted to know just generally regarding the findings of your report if you could compare your results with respect to Islamic monuments and Orthodox and Catholic monuments that are depicted there on the map.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The Islamic monuments suffered the greatest damage during the war. The damage in the summer of 1998, the first cycle of armed conflict was relatively more limited, I think about 40 different sites got hit then. The bulk of the damage to the Islamic heritage occurred between March and June of 1999. In terms of the Serbian Orthodox heritage, we could find no confirmation that any Orthodox monuments had been damaged before June of 1999, but then at the end of hostilities, as the Albanian refugees started returning, the Serbian security forces were withdrawing from Kosovo. There was a wave of attacks on Serbian churches and monasteries during the first several months after the end of the war. The Catholic heritage was relatively unaffected by the war, with the exception of a small number of churches in the west of Kosovo right near the Albanian border and in the Klina area in the north, just east of Pec. There were a few Albanian village churches that got damaged or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And with respect to the Islamic heritage, based on what you were able to observe and upon the information you obtained from the sources while you were conducting this survey, were there any areas that were more affected than others by this time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at this map, and there are also maps that separate out the various damage, but if you will look at the distribution of the red dots which represent the Islamic heritage on this map, you will see certain areas where there was virtually no damage. Quite obviously, first of all, there are areas where there were very few mosques to begin with because they were primarily Serbian population. So the far north of Kosovo, the area around Strpce in the south, and in the far east, where again it's mixed population. The one area where the population is overwhelmingly Muslim but not Albanian is -- stands out; it's the far southern tip of Kosovo around Brod and Dragas. There the population are Gorani, who are Muslim Slavs. They are Muslims. Every village has a mosque, but they had good relations with the Belgrade authorities and not a single mosque in those villages was damaged during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I would like to move to a different exhibit. This is Exhibit 01799, if we could have that up on the screen. And this is a set of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have that before you, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a photo of the Charshi, or market mosque, in Vucitrn. It's a town north of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was this one of the photographs that you obtained while you were conducting your survey?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a pre-war photo taken in late 1998 by a local historian Raif Virmica just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we move to page 2 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, while this is coming up on the screen, yesterday when you were explaining how you conducted the survey you spoke about assessment of damage and how you would grade the damage in each site, and I would just -- we're going to go through a series of photographs, but I would just ask you, using this as an example, if you could explain to the Chamber how you went about grading the damage that you observed at each site. And if you could first tell us what is depicted here in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are looking at approximately the same vantage point. This is what remained of this mosque after the war. In the foreground you can see rubble. In the background you can see intact apartment buildings. If Your Honours will observe at the top left quadrant of the screen, there is an apartment building that is yellowish and brownish with a triangular cable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There is a pen on the side of the screen if you wish to point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe the usher could assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you could just mark it and that way we can see what you're pointing at.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This apartment building can also be seen in the pre-war photo which allows you to orient yourself to see what you're looking at. If you switch back to the pre-war photo, I can point that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think we first need to have this admitted before we move to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this marked photo will be P01100.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is a photo that I took in October of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this would have been one of the sites you visited?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now move back to the first photograph we were looking at earlier. It's page 1 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will now mark the same apartment building. It's not doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There. I think now you can mark.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you can see it in the background immediately to the left of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I had asked you earlier if you could explain to Your Honours how you graded the damage in each of the sites that you visited, if we could use this as an example.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. If you will take a close look at where the mosque is, to the left of the mosque are some concrete steps that go up to an ablution fountain which is used for people to wash themselves before praying. If you go to the post-war picture, you will see the remnants of the concrete steps and to the right you will see just the bare foundations of the mosque rubble. This is an example of our top damage category, completely destroyed. There is no element of the building remaining above ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In addition to that category, did you use other categories to grade damage that you observed --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- at each of these sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we -- Mr. Herscher and I, before setting out on our field trip to Kosovo, established damage categories which were modelled after damage categories used by UNHCR and by heritage authorities before the war. We tried to make it as simple as possible so they would be based on observational criteria and not require technical testing, for which we had neither the equipment nor the time. The lowest level of damage category obviously is intact, undamaged, meaning a building does not show any signs of damage or any signs of recent repairs or reconstruction. The next category of damage is lightly damaged. The lightly damaged is a category that we used very conservatively, meaning that a building was called lightly damaged as long as no principal structural element of the building had been impaired. So a building that had had the top of the minaret shot off or a hole in the wall would still be called lightly damaged. The next category would be seriously damaged or severely damaged. That category would involve usually impairment -- structural impairment of one or more of the main elements of the building itself. Often this would be compound damage. A building would be missing its roof, part of a wall fallen in. Usually this would be a building that would require extensive or complete reconstruction. The next category is almost destroyed. This is a building where almost all of the elements had been damaged or destroyed but there were still visible elements of the building standing above ground. So, for example, you know, if part of a wall is still standing or part of a minaret is still sticking up, that would be almost destroyed if the rest of the building was unsalvageable. And we have here the top category, which is completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to move to page 3 of this exhibit, but before we do that I would like to tender this marked photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01101.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recognise the structure that's depicted here in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is another photograph that I took. It's another mosque in Vucitrn. It's the oldest mosque in Vucitrn, the mosque of Gazi Ali-beg. You can see that the minaret has been sheered off and has fallen on top of the mosque, smashing part of the roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How would you grade this type of damage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This we called lightly damaged still. Because as you can see only part of the roof has been stove-in and the main part of the building is still standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we go to the next photograph -- next page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And could you comment on this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the third mosque in Vucitrn, the Karamanli mosque. It dates from the 17th century. Once again the minaret has been sheered off. We actually had an informant who stated that he watched a tank or armoured vehicle come up to the immediate vicinity of the mosque and shoot at the minaret, causing it to collapse. As you can see, it smashed a considerable portion of the roof, and I was initially proposing that we call this severely damaged. And Mr. Herscher and I had an argument about it and he insisted that we call it lightly damaged. And since he's the architect, I deferred to him. So we classed that as lightly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we see the next photograph in this exhibit, page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a view of the interior of that mosque, showing part of the collapsed minaret and collapsed roof which fell into the interior after it smashed through the roof structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is also a site that you personally visited?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same one as before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to tender this set of five photographs into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 01799 will be Exhibit P01102.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now please have Exhibit 02456 up on the screen. And, Your Honours, while this is being brought up I just wanted to explain that I'm going to be showing a number of attachments to the report during my examination. These have been uploaded as separate exhibits in our e-court system simply because the copy of the report and the attachments in e-court do not contain any coloured photographs and it's very difficult to make out what is depicted in the photographs. So there is some overlap or some duplication between these exhibits that I will be showing and the ones that are already part of the report. I'm just explaining that for purpose of clarity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't know if you have that up on your screen.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It hasn't been displayed yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe I can provide the witness with a hard copy while we're waiting for that to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We don't have the exhibit yet, but it's the 65 ter -- oh, I think it's coming up.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain what this is, this document we have here.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have is the part of the entry from the database that we compiled as part of the report for the monument we just saw in the previous exhibit. Would you like me to explain the categories?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We constructed this form in order to assist the Court if there were witnesses, for example, we would put in any variant forms of the name of the mosque. Here they all look very similar. And some mosques, they have multiple names which don't resemble each other. Then we would put in the name of the town and the district in Serbian and Albanian. We carried a GPS device and took readings whenever we stopped at a site in order to make it possible for anyone to go and check. We put in the date of construction and restoration, the historical period, the category where there is a religious building, civic building, and so forth. Then the type of the building, in this case a mosque. The setting, where there is city, village, or country-side. The setting relationship is an architectural term that has to do whether it is an asset to the site or sticks out like an eye sore. This is mainly to assist the planning authorities who were, sort of, the other audience for our survey. Then the building condition, lightly damaged and under reconstruction, they were clearing the rubble when we got there. Occupancy speaks for itself, that it was in use. And we always made a point of examining other buildings adjacent to it to see whether they were damaged. That gives some indication of whether a building has been singled out or whether it is part of a more widespread pattern of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, underneath the photograph we have the name of Sabri Bajgora. Could you explain who he was?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while the witness is doing that, if we could have the second page displayed since this exhibit seems to be taking some time in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Sabri -- or who is Mr. Sabri Bajgora?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sabri Bajgora is the deputy mufti of Kosovo and at the end of the conflict he took it upon himself to travel throughout the area and visit the various Islamic congregations that are part of the Islamic Community of Kosovo, of which he was deputy head at the time, and he took photographs and also collected photographs from local people documenting the damage. When we arrived in Kosovo, our first task was to visit various people who might have documentation ranging from the monuments authority to the various religious communities. When we visited the Islamic Community's headquarters in Pristina, he showed us his photographs and first offered to give us a CD. And I asked him if he could have the originals so there would be no question that these were not manipulated photographs but the actual prints, which I have in my archive. I used his photograph in this case because it shows the site immediately at the end of the war. By the time we got there, some of the rubble had been cleaned up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. We can look at the second page which is now being displayed. It's the back of the sheet you have there. There is a section called "Informant Statements" and I would just like to ask you if you could explain how that information that's contained there was collected by you or obtained by you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived at this site, as in many other cases when we arrived at a site, started taking photographs. A crowd gathered. This gentleman here, Mr. Azim Xhyshinca owned a shop across the corner from the mosque and he volunteered that he had been in his shop and watched as the mosque was destroyed. So we took down the basics of what he said. It's not a verbatim statement but a summary that we wrote down as he spoke and then took his contact information in case there was any interest in contacting him further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have page 3 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while that's being done, could you explain what impact these external sources had in your assessment of the damage to the different sites that you visited if any.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The external sources meaning the statements from other --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: From other persons.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had no impact on the assessment of the damage. The damage was entirely on visual criteria. But if the information was there, we included it in order to assist the Court if they wanted to follow it up and to give it whatever degree of credence they wish to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, and here we see on this page you have a section called "Bibliography" which began on the bottom of the last page and it's on the top of this page. Was that material you relied on?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bibliography, meaning both before we went to Kosovo and after we came back, I did extensive library research. Before we went to Kosovo the reason I did that is looking for pre-destruction photographs and ground-plans. The ground-plans turned out to be extremely useful in the cases of buildings which had been completely destroyed, where you could follow-up the foundation outlines. Pre-destruction photographs could equally be useful because they often showed features in the background that one could match up. And so these often appeared in publications. The other use of the bibliography of the publications is that they give some indications of what were the historically important buildings that we should check out what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see there's also a section called "Media Accounts" which in this particular form has been left empty. I think you have explained earlier how you relied on media accounts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P01103.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now move to Exhibit 01797. And if I could have my copy back from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the historical centre of the town of Djakovica or Gjakova in Albanian, a town in western Kosovo. You see in the foreground the burnt-out shops of the historic bazaar, and in the centre rear you see the Hadum mosque. It's a 16th century mosque at the centre of the bazaar and you can see that its minaret has been sheered off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is this also a site that you personally visited?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we see page 2 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you explain what is depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the same historic bazaar taken just before the war by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Kosovo. It was used as part of an exhibit held at the beginning of 1999 in Thessaloniki in which the Yugoslav government participated. It was part of a European conference on the conservation of medieval markets and the negatives were still in Pristina and we got a copy of the prints.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to tender these two photographs, Your Honours, 01797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01104.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have Exhibit 01781 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is once again the database entry for the historic bazaar in Djakovica or Gjakova. You see the Albanian, Serbian, and English names of the bazaar on top, and you can see our assessment which is that it was heavily damaged. You see the photographs. You see the same pre-war photograph on top. The next photograph down we got from a news agency. It was taken by a local resident the day of the burning of the bazaar and shows part of the bazaar on fire. At the right is the damage description.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In the section on damage description, I believe that's photograph 4, there's -- you refer to: "Yugoslav authorities having claimed that the damage to the bazaar and the Hadum mosque were caused by NATO strikes." Could you comment on that information that you received based on your observations when you were on site.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the claim came in the Yugoslav government's White Book which was issued in two volumes in 1999 containing various allegations on destruction in -- during the war. We checked out each of these allegations, including this one. And here both the pattern of the destruction and the nature of the destruction seem to suggest that this was destruction that had happened by fire from the ground up rather than as a result of destruction by the air-strikes. Neither of us is a military expert, however we observed that over a widespread area along the streets of the bazaar, all the shops fronting the street were burned out. The shops basically had only their separation walls left standing, but the separation walls for the most part were undamaged and the interior with all combustible material was destroyed. There was no sign of any blast damage. Normally you would expect rubble to be scattered, and we saw no sign of that. We also managed to obtain photographs of the bazaar taken immediately after the war in June and July before there had been any clean-up. And you could see -- you could draw some fairly good common-sense conclusions from the nature of the damage. The other thing that struck us was the distribution of the damage. The damage seemed to be confined to the shops immediately fronting the street. There were certain buildings, a few of them that were left intact. But otherwise, for an extent of several blocks, all of them were damaged, yet the houses behind the shops in the neighbourhood adjacent to it were, for the most part, untouched. And once again, one would have expected if there had been such widespread damage from an air-strike that there would have been also some damage that would have spread away from the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can see page 2 of this, top of page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to obtaining photographs from July. I just wanted to know if the photographs we see here to the left is one of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is from July of 1999. This is as returning residents were cleaning up the rubble immediately after their return. The source of the photograph was Mr. Xhavit Lokaj. Xhavit Lokaj was employed by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Pristina -- of Kosovo in Pristina. And he travelled through Kosovo during that summer and took a lot of photos which he was willing to share with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. It's 01781 and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01105.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have 02455 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, sir; and if yes, could you please comment? And if you would like to make any markings, you can use the pen you have there.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an aerial or satellite photograph showing the same area that we just discussed. It was -- is posted on the US Department of Defence web site. I believe it's still available. And I simply downloaded it. It was posted in response to a -- an allegation by the Belgrade government that on the first night of the war the Hadum mosque, which is at the centre of the photograph here, and the surrounding bazaar had been destroyed by NATO bombing. And so the photograph was displayed as an effort to show, A, that the mosque was intact; and B, that the bazaar was burning, but that it was not the result of bombing. I conclude nothing from the claims, but the picture shown here corresponds very largely to what we saw on our visit. This was taken at the end of March 1999 on our visit in October 1999 on the ground. You can see up and down this street here and along here destruction of shops. You can see shops that are missing their roofs. You can see the separation walls between them. And you can also see the neighbourhood behind essentially undamaged. The mosque itself isn't damaged but there is smoke rising from buildings adjacent to the mosque. Right next to the mosque is the library of the Hadum mosque, and it appears that smoke is drifting out of that. Across from it, here, is an Islamic school which also was -- when we got there was completely ruined and the locals said it was burning. The one additional damage we saw which is not visible on this photograph is one side of this street was also burned out when we got there. The city of Djakovica is -- has two rivers, a smaller river here running from the north -- running north and south which separates the eastern part of town, which is the more modern area, from the traditional centre. And then in the south of the town is the Ereniku River which eventually runs into the Beli Drim, the main river in the west of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the transcript, the witness has drawn a circle to indicate the location of the mosque. He drew a first line to the left of that circle from the top to the bottom of the photograph to indicate where shops where that he observed destroyed. And he also drew a second line on the top of the circle marking the mosque, also to indicate another street where shops were destroyed. He has made a marking to the left of the circle right adjacent to it to indicate the location of the library and has made an additional marking to the right of the location of the mosque, a larger circle to indicate another area where he saw destruction when he visited the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01106.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter 01796 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the front of the Hadum mosque at the centre of the old bazaar in Djakovica. This is another one of the photographs taken by Xhavit Lokaj immediately at the end of the war, but it looked essentially the same when we visit in October of 1999. To the right you see the mosque. And if you will consult the database later you will see that originally the mosque has an extended wooden portico that extended maybe one and a half times the distance of the remaining stone portico. All the wooden material has been burned. You can see immediately to the right of the dome the base of the minaret. From that other photo you saw that the top of the minaret had been severed. To the left here you can see part of the ruins of the Islamic school. And to the right of the mosque you can see the front half of the mosque library which was a separate building, and the back of the library was completely gone. I believe we will see a second picture of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this Exhibit. It's 01796.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01107.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The next document I would like to have up is 01782, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We have another entry from your database, and I would just like to ask you to comment on this one.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again you see the standard elements of our database, including the assessment of the building condition, which is heavily damaged. In this case there are multiple elements of the mosque that were impaired. The portico had been burned down, the minaret had been severed above the muezzins balcony. Parts of the rubble had fallen on the dome damaging that. You see a general picture from a slightly more distant view than we just saw before. That is one of the photographs I got from Mr. Bajgora. Down below you see a close-up of the portico itself. And to the right you see the damage description.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we see page 2 of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to note from the previous page - you don't need to screen back - at the bottom right it said "surveyor Andrew Herscher." In fact, we visited each site together. The person who got to sign it as surveyor was simply the person who was taking the notes usually while the other person was holding the camera, so it's interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see here that there's a photograph taken by you on site during your visit?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, and it shows the base of the minaret which is heavily charred by fire. You can see at the left the portico of the mosque. At the right you can see the front facade of the library and you can see right through it because the back of the building is missing. And at the right from a book published in 1998 you can see what the portico looked like immediately before the war as well as the minaret with the top still on it. You can see that in front of the three small domes of the stone portico there is a large extension. The reason for this, this is found in many mosques in the Balkans, is that the climate is fairly severe. And when there is a large congregation, as on a Muslim holiday which are movable feasts and therefore occur during the winter in some years, as well as for funerals, there will be large crowds and they need shelter from the weather. So in many cases old mosques had these wooden extensions put on. This one dates from the early 19th century.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this Exhibit. It's 01782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P01108.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The next paragraph I want to move to is 01795, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And could you comment on this photograph, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a view of the mosque library taken from the rear of the library. To your right you see the base of the minaret and you can see that the building has essentially been chopped in half. Both on my -- this particular photograph was taken immediately after the war by Mr. Bajgora, but this is exactly what the building looked like at the time of our October 1999 visit. Both at that time and at later -- on two subsequent visits, I inspected the rubble inside and found elements of the minaret that were recognisable, such as parts of the carved stone balcony of the minaret -- of the minaret balcony where the prayer call is issued from which were in the rubble. As you can also see, the interior has signs of charring. The little niches in the walls are where the books were kept. The library had two levels, separated by a wooden floor, which is gone. And we could see charred bits of wood where the floor had been anchored in the walls. The informant statement told us that the damage to the library had occurred in two phases. The library itself had been burned at the same time that the wooden portico had been burned at the beginning of the war in March of 1999, and the minaret had been decapitated in early May of 1999. And that's when the rear of the library was sheered off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for clarity, you were talking about a library adjacent to the same mosque we were looking at earlier, the Hadum mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the library also dates from the 16th century, although this particular building is from the early 18th century.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this photograph. It's 01795.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01109.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could have 01783 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we'll just look at this very briefly, again, an entry from your database.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you scroll down. The building is classed as heavily damaged and that needs no further explanation in this case. If you scroll down, perhaps the next page, the informant statement contains the information about what was in the library and how it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this would have been a person you spoke to personally while you were --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both of these cases these were people I spoke to. The information on the contents of the library came from Professor Nexhat Krasniqi. He is the keeper of rare books and manuscripts at the National University Library in Pristina. And so he informed me that there had been about 200 manuscripts and 1500 old and rare books in the library. And the information as left came from Mr. Xhahit Bashe, B-a-s-h-e, he turned up as I was taking pictures of the mosque, introduced himself as a senior member of the mosque congregation, and gave the information you saw there about how the library was burned and how the damaged occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on your observations on site, this was all one part of one same complex, the mosque and library were all one same --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all the foundation of Hadum Sulejmani who was a native of the region who rose to high rank in the Ottoman Empire and who endowed these buildings, the school, the library, and the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this into evidence, Your Honour. It's 01783.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01110.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have P614 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap for the sake of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building depicted in the photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the white mosque or Xhamija Bardhe in Suva Reka, which is a small town north of Prizren. This is a picture that Mr. Herscher took. What you can see here is the entrance of the mosque, and if you take a careful look on the right you will see signs of damage. At the right is where the minaret was, no longer is at this point, and you can see some damage to the domes next to the minaret due to the destruction of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now move to the next page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're looking at the same building. Basically we've gone around the right-hand corner of the building. At the left of the photo you can see the side of the front portico and you can see here the base of the minaret. You can see that the minaret has been destroyed, and you can see some signs of how it might have been destroyed. This -- I took this from standing next to it from the outside, and you can see that the base of the minaret has basically been ballooned outwards. Parts of it are sticking out. Every minaret is a hollow tube with a staircase going up the centre, and it seems very evident, to me at least, that there was an explosion inside the minaret that pushed it outwards. This was confirmed when I went inside the mosque and you can see on top an opening. The minaret was entered from the women's balcony inside the mosque. Traditional mosque like Orthodox Jewish synagogues have the women separate from the men on a balcony above the entrance and the entrance to the minaret was from the women's balcony. And standing on the women's balcony you could see radiating signs of blast, meaning there were scorch marks on the wall and parts of the balcony had been damaged, so, again, confirming that there had been an explosion inside the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I would to move to another exhibit, this exhibit is already in evidence. It's 01779.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is again an entry from your database. And we see on this entry one of the photographs that was just shown to you. I wanted your comments on one sentence that's under the damage heading, which is the second paragraph which says: "Minaret blown up by Serbs on Bajram (Muslim holiday, 28th of March ..." If you could just tell us how you obtained that information.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will scroll down, I don't know if it's possible, you will see the source of the information which came from the informant --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think that's on the next page in this version in e-court. And --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as I recall in this case, we had -- oops, that's a little too far. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's page 2. I think we're on page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just go ahead. You were ...

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The gentleman who -- here you have it, yes. The gentleman who gave us the information -- oh, here you see the picture from the inside of the women's balcony at the left. Right below it is the informant statement. The gentleman who gave the statement was a local resident who had a house across the street from the mosque and who told us that on the 28th of March, which was the day of the Bajram, the major Muslim holiday, the Albanians in town were forbidden to leave their houses. And at noon he heard a large explosion and he looked out and the minaret was gone. So that is part of where the information came from. We also spoke to the imam of the mosque, who is quoted in one of the media accounts below, and he confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we saw on the first page that the damage to this mosque was graded as lightly damaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, because the principal structure was not really severely affected. The minaret is gone, but the minaret is a subsidiary element of the building. What makes it tragic in this case is that it was a very old mosque to begin with, but in very bad shape. And just before the war, the main structure of the mosque had been completely rebuilt and the only historic part remaining was the minaret. And so now that is gone as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this into evidence. It's 01779. I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01111.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have P634 up on the screen, and this is, again, a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a pre-war photo of the mosque in the village of Celine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was this one of the photographs you obtained from one of your sources?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was supplied by Dr. Xhabir Hamiti who is the secretary of the Islamic Community of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now move to 65 ter 01800, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, do you know approximately when that photograph that we just saw was taken, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was taken before the war is all I was told. So I assume 1998 or earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recognise this site that is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same mosque, a picture taken after the war. The photograph in this case came from Mr. Bajgora, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to tell that this was the same site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first I was told it was the same site, and it's a little hard looking at the post-destruction photo to even tell that it was a mosque. However, the one recognisable element in the photo is that semicircular structure in the centre --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would you mind using your pen to indicate it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here. If you look at it carefully, first of all, you can see it's arched shape and that it is concrete with bricks inserted on their end, at the outer perimeter, an ornamental feature. And upon examination of the photo and the previous photo, I conclude that this is part of the minaret balcony. If you can flip back to the previous photo I can show you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We first need to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this marked photograph will be Exhibit P01112.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the previous photograph we were looking at is P634, if we could have that back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is this again a site you visited yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Celine is not one of the sites we visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you did your assessment on the damage, would that have been based on the photographs you received?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you could indicate what you were trying to explain earlier on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part I circled is the bottom of the balcony. This is a fairly recent mosque. I'm told it was built around the 1970s. The main body of the minaret is made of reinforced concrete and the balcony was the only decorated element. And the -- in this case the balcony just had a metal railing, but the bottom of the balcony had the ornamentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this marked photograph, Your Honours, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01113.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have 01773 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, again, an entry from your database. You have already explained the structure of these entries. I just wanted to ask you about one of the institutions here -- or sources listed as surveyor, the EU/IMG database. If you could explain what that is just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: IMG stands for International Management Group. It is an inter-governmental organisation which was commissioned by the European Community to conduct a survey of damage to infrastructure in Kosovo after the 1999 war. And they set up teams in every Kosovo municipality, with the task of essentially documenting infrastructure. Their focus was on public facilities such as schools, hospitals, bridges, and so forth; but fortunately they also included among their categories cultural infrastructure, one element of which was houses of worship. And so they were willing to share their database with us even though it was produced internally. It was not a published document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did this database contain photographs of the destroyed sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Each entry had one or more photographs, it also had basic categories of description, both when the date of construction was, what the construction materials were, and then categories, some of which didn't really fit historic buildings very well, such as: Did it have sewage connections or, you know, electric power or telephone link, because their focus really was on modern public buildings. But for us the most part was the photographs. Because they had large local staff they could cover much broader area than we were in condition to do. I must explain that although Kosovo is a relatively small territory, the roads were in terrible shape and some of the villages were extremely remote. And it would have taken hours and a four-wheel drive vehicle to get to some of them. So we were very fortunate to have photographs of places that we couldn't go to. And because this was managed under the auspices of the European Union by professionals, we had some confidence that at least the photographs depicted what they say they depicted. We had a -- slightly more reservations about the way the damage description was structured. And maybe if you can show an entry from their database, I can explain that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We will get to that later.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At this stage, Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 01773.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01114.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have 02444 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would just ask you to explain what this document that's going to come up is. If you could just very briefly tell us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This is an extract from the cadastral register for the municipality of Orahovac, or Rahovec in Albanian. The cadastral register is basically the land records. And this was obtained for me by Mr. Xhabir Hamiti the secretary of the Islamic Community. What it is is the record for the mosque at Celine which it gives basic description as to what -- how many square metres the building is, how many square metres the plot of ground is, and its owner is the Islamic Community of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 02444.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01115.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The next document is 01806, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is depicted on this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is a photograph that I took. It's the mosque at the village of Rogovo, which is south of Djakovica. It's a 16th century monument. And what you're looking at is the remains of the minaret. You can see part of the staircase exposed right below the big gap in the building. And you can also see that the minaret has collapsed onto the building. You can see the damage to the dome, cracks to the main structure. And on the left was a portico with domes on it that has also been crushed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this photograph, Your Honours. It's 01806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01116.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could now move 01784, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is again an entry from your database. I would just ask you very briefly to comment on the two photographs that we see at the bottom of the page. If we could zoom in.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct something I said just before -- the portico which is actually grouped around the courtyard didn't have domes, it had a tile roof. I misspoke. You have here -- the first photo you saw was taken from the right-hand side where the minaret used to be, and here you can see some of the damage to the portico roof as well, but also the fact that the minaret is not there. And the photo below is a pre-war photo from 1997, which shows the minaret still intact. That's one of the photographs we got from the -- from a local historian named Raif Virmica, who allowed us to take copies of his photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I see that under the heading "Damage" it says: "Attack on mosque took place on 3rd April, 1999, according to village residents." Did you personally have the opportunity to speak to residents?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were rather vague about it because nobody claimed to have witnessed it personally, but the owner of the shop across the street from the mosque named a woman in a village several miles away that allegedly saw it. I put down that information, vague as it was, in case somebody needed to track it down. But I wouldn't place very great reliance on the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now move to 00098.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And again, sir, this is a photograph and I would ask you to just comment on what is depicted there. I see that that is up on the screen. And if you need to indicate anything I would ask you to use the pen that you have there.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]

You can see the main dome of the mosque to the right of the minaret and the entry of the mosque with three small domes to the left of the minaret. The picture on the right says that it is the building. In order to understand it you have to understand also that the angle is reversed. If you look at the curve of the river, this is coming the other direction. If you look at the three little domes, they face the river in both pictures. And the conspicuous difference is that, first of all, you can see the village houses all around no longer have roofs and the mosque no longer has a minaret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please draw a circle just to indicate where the mosque is on the photograph to the right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just for the sake of the transcript the witness drew a circle on the photograph on the left, a large circle, to indicate the location of the mosque and smaller circles within that circle to indicate the domes. And he's also drawn a circle in the photograph -- on the photograph to the right to indicate the location where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this marked photograph into evidence. It's 00098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P01118.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have 01792 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, the dates that are shown on this photograph that we just saw are those dates that were available on the web site when you consulted it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The photo was as taken from the web site.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a picture of the same mosque taken from the ground. And I don't recall for certain, but I believe it's another one from Mr. Bajgora. And what you see here is the large dome of the mosque at the right of the building and the three small domes, one of them completely crushed to the left of it. And the big gap in the centre of the building is where the minaret was. Generally in the Balkans the custom is to put the minaret to the right of the entrance. So the entrance of the building is at the far left and the minaret would have been on the right side of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this photograph. It's 01792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time or are you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: One more exhibit in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One more, all right, we'll manage one more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So it's 01774.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is, again, an entry from your database. We see one of the photographs is a photograph we just saw and there's a second photograph below that.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that shows the damage to the interior. What you're looking at is the prayer niche. And the minaret would have been to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see under the section "Damage" you have noted that this: "Village site of atrocity is cited in Milosevic et al. indictment." Why did you include this information in this entry?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we did our survey, we were not looking for atrocities; however, as an assist to the Court, when we looked at cultural damage and it happened to coincide with sites mentioned in the indictment, we would note it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 01774, and this is a convenient time to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have a break at this point for the tapes to be rewound, and we resume in half an hour at 11.00. The Court Officer will assist you in the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- yesterday I made an oral application to add four photographs for the Cirez site. I was wondering if -- what Your Honours' position was on that matter since I'm going to be shortly moving to that site and would like to use those photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, we're to hear you on this, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As I promised yesterday and today, in connection with the additional information received from the witness, I personally believe that these -- this evidence could not be used at this stage of the proceedings, particularly from the time that the report was drafted to today. So much time has passed so that we no longer know what the reason is to provide these photographs and the sources, Human Rights Watch, are quite unreliable. Because in his testimony in the Milutinovic case this witness to an explicit question from one of my learned colleagues whether he cooperated with any non-governmental organisations in obtaining the documents, being explicitly asked whether he cooperated with Human Rights Watch said, Never. He said he only cooperated with the Doctors for Human Rights, that was the only organisation. So the origin of these photographs is to be questioned, and just to say that Human Rights Watch is the source without the author, the time the photographs were taken, and so on, and other information I believe is so problematic that this could not be used as evidence in this case. So the Defence is opposed to having this evidence admitted into evidence and against this material being used in evidence for this case. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information that my learned colleague is -- has just provided is not entirely accurate. We provided assist to the Defence earlier this week, regarding the source of each one of the photographs. These are not photographs, all of them, from Human Rights Watch. There is only one, I believe it's the first one, which was obtained by the witness. He indicated when he came in -- to proofing earlier in the week that he had obtained these photographs just before coming and that is the reason why he had not provided them to the Office of the Prosecution earlier. I believe that the source of two of the other photographs is UNHCR and there's one from a local source. However, I believe the witness is in a better position than I am to explain how he obtained the four photographs and where exactly -- who provided them to him, if it was each one of these organisations or if it was a third party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, these four photographs can be added to the Rule 65 ter list. As you come to use each one, if you would be kind enough to indicate they're one of the four photographs subject of this motion. We will hear what the witness has to say about the source of the photograph, and we will then hear anything that might be raised in cross-examination in respect. And a final decision can then be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry delayed you for a moment. We had a procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now have 65 ter 01802 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise, sir, what is depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I do. It's a pre-war photo of a mosque next to the bridge in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this one of the sites you visited while conducting your survey?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we see page 2 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you explain what is depicted here.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the site of the mosque after the war. It is a photo I have I believe from Xhavit Lokaj, and it looked the same when I visited Mitrovica, but that wasn't until 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how -- from whom did you obtain information at this site, because we see there is nothing there at the site? There was the mosque that we had seen in the earlier photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to the site, I was taken there by the imam of the mosque and he explained that this is where the mosque was. As you say, there isn't much one can tell. There are bits of rubble and the location certainly fits the location where the mosque used to be with regard to street address.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender these two photographs as a 65 ter 01802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01121.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could now move to 01780, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry from your database.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could zoom in towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to make two corrections to my previous observation. It looks like the photo came from Mr. Bajgora, not Xhavit Lokaj, and in fact my visit to Mitrovica was my second return visit in March of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why is it that you did not visit this site during your first trip in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe I mentioned earlier this morning or maybe yesterday, we were advised by the ICTY field office in Pristina that they had received information from KFOR that there was going to be trouble in Mitrovica the day we had planned to go to Mitrovica, and in fact that was when the first riot, confrontation, took place at the bridge which is right next to this mosque. So we were told it was inadvisable to go to Mitrovica that day. In March of 2001, I had a commission from the UNMIK department of culture to carry out an assessment of the public library in Mitrovica, so I took that opportunity to visit the sites, although I had photographs in hand already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see from the damage description that it says that the site has been completely razed. That is consistent with your observation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the top part of this entry indicates that this site has been graded as being "completely destroyed."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, under the "Damage" heading there's also a sentence that refers to the date of when the damage to the mosque was carried out, and this would have been --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information from the Islamic Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Of the town of Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 01780.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P01122.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now move to 01803.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the mosque in the village of Landovica, which is just north of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you personally visit this site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you just provide us with information as to your observations that you --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph was taken --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The photograph was taken from the main highway itself, just from the verge of the highway, which is immediately next to the mosque. The -- what you see in the picture is the part of the minaret that has been toppled. I also took other pictures of the mosque. The minaret is a modern minaret, and it came apart in pieces. One of the pieces seems to have crashed into the dome which had a big hole in it, and -- otherwise, the building looked intact except for the windows being gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this photograph, Your Honours. It's 01803.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01123.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz is kindly asked to speak up for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies for that. If I could now have 01777 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, again, an entry from your database.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]

The interior photo came from Mr. Bajgora which shows the hole before it had been patched. utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see under "Surveyor" that the date given there is October 1999. That would have been the date when you visited the site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01124.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could move to 01785.01, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see this same photograph that has -- that we've just seen earlier. If you can just comment on the damage, the information contained there under the heading "Damage."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had an exterior photo of the building where you cannot see much evidence of damage, but the interior was clearly burned out. utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 of this exhibit. And if we could just zoom in the photograph we see there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this what you were referring to earlier when --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- you were speaking about -- so would this have been the state in August of 1999 when the photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this exhibit, Your Honour, into evidence as 01785.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a site I visited. It's definitely in my database.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But without reference to it, I -- for the moment I'm having a lapse as to which one of those it is. It's one of several villages in that area just north of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have up on the screen 01776.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which is an entry from your database.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers are kindly asked not to overlap for the sake of interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.text: Sir, we're being reminded that we need to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. My second guess was correct, it is Velika Krusa. It is again a picture of the mosque and of the site where the minaret was, the big gap in the side of the building. The photos in this case came from Mr. Bajgora, but once again there was independent confirmation from the EU/IMG database as well as from media accounts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender these two exhibits. The one currently up on the screen is 01776, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01127.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The previous photograph was 01794, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P01128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now move to 01793, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recognise this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is the mosque at Brestovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall -- was this a site you visited or --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
