utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on the -- on what we observe in the photograph, what were your conclusions regarding the damage suffered?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the photographs, first of all, the building is completely gutted, it's burned out, and the top of the minaret is missing. And I believe we classified it as "heavily damaged."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 01793.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P01129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I just have a brief question regarding this exhibit. This is an entry from your database. We see that this entry relates to Brestovac and we see the same photograph that you just commented on. Under the heading "Damage" there's -- the second line says: "According to Islamic Community, the mosque was destroyed on March 25th, 1999." Was this information you personally obtained?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obtained the information from the Islamic Community in Orahovac, which is the centre for the area in which the village of Brestovac is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you did travel to the municipality but not to this specific --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the village, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. And we see again that this photograph was provided by Mr. Sabri Bajgora. He's not a member of that particular --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's a member of the -- all Kosovo Islamic Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 01775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01130.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now look at 01786, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry from your database for the town of Kotlina. Could you explain why there is no photograph attached in this entry. Was it because you were unable to obtain photographs or was there another reason?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did have a photograph from the EU/IMG database, but for technical reasons I couldn't extract the photograph from the IMG database and put it into my database. But I did provide the Tribunal with the IMG database.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very remote village, and it was not one we were able to travel to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And so your assessment on the building condition -- oh, I see the document, it's on the right of the screen. Your assessment regarding the condition of the building was then made on the basis of that photograph from the --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- IMG database if I understand correctly? Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this entry. It's 01786.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01131.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can now move to 05341. And, Your Honours, these are the four photographs that we had spoken about earlier before the witness came in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these are photographs you brought with you when you came earlier in the week. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a photograph of the mosque in the village of Cirez. This particular photograph came from Human Rights Watch and was taken immediately after the end of the war. Would you like me to comment on what it shows?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a view from where the interior of the mosque used to be, the main prayer hall, which is now completely destroyed. And you're looking out through the front door. The three small domes were over the entrance, and you can see that two of them are damaged. The arch in front of you is all that remains of the main prayer hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if you could comment on these two photographs that are shown here.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are photographs of the same mosque taken in April of 1998 during the Muslim Bajram, the major feast. The photos were taken by the local congregation, and they were obtained for me very recently by Mr. Xhabir Hamiti, the -- who has now recently been elected the president of the Assembly of the Islamic Community of Kosovo. He used to be the secretary. The photograph is particularly useful because it shows the entire mosque. And you can see the main prayer hall with a very large dome and the three small domes over the entrance in that odd, slightly staggered configuration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can move to page 3 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, again, I would ask for your comments on the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph also came from Mr. Xhabir Hamiti, and it shows the mosque after the war. The photo is taken from the entrance facade. You can see again the three small domes. And what you don't see is the main prayer hall of the mosque which had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a photograph from the UN Commission for Human Rights. It was taken during a trip commissioned by UNHCR by the Canadian photographer Roger Lemoyne, that's L-e-m-o-y-n-e, and it shows the interior of the mosque in October of 1998 being used as shelter for refugees at the end of the first summer of fighting. What it shows, of course, is that as of then the main prayer hall was still intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender these four photographs. I know there has been an objection raised by the Defence, but I believe the witness has already explained the source of each one of the photographs. It's 65 ter 05341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification. Unless you have a change --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's fine, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01132 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now have 01778 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry from your database. I would just ask you to comment on the section below "Building Condition" and "Damage."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the photos we had in hand at the time of our -- when we prepared our report, and unfortunately they were not as easy to read as the others before. But if you look at it very carefully you will see that the top photo shows the mosque taken from the side to the right of the entrance. You can see the -- at the right-hand side of the photo the collapsed remnants of the main prayer hall. Then you can see the first and a little bit of the second of the three domes taken from the side of the three small domes of the entrance and the still-standing part of the portico. And below is a photo taken from the entrance side showing the mosque before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is this the same mosque that we saw in the other photographs --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- that you just commented on. We see that you're not listed under the heading "Surveyor," but did you have the opportunity to visit this site during your trips to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We passed the mosque on the way back from a trip to western Kosovo, but it was too dark to take a picture and I was hoping we would get photos from elsewhere. But I did not list myself as a surveyor in this case because we did not in fact stop to make a close inspection. It was getting dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help us a little. The lower of the two photographs indicates a two-level, two-storey building, whereas the other photograph seem to suggest only one level. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, if you look at it, Your Honour, on the bottom of the -- on the bottom photograph, the arcade has a side window which is what you see there. The top level seems to have collapsed somehow. I don't know -- if we went back to the other photos maybe we could get a better sense of what is going on in the previous ones Ms. Kravetz showed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 05341, which is the document that we have just viewed and was marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could see page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this the same building that we were just looking at in your database entry?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is, and if you also get the next page which shows the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- destruction, you can see that the second level has collapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's your understanding these photographs are of the same building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that they are all of the same building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is some concern that the scale and structure appear to differ in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well -- okay, again, I would draw Your Honours' attention to the characteristic window on the right-hand side of the arcade, and if we could go back to the pre-war photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is page 2 of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, you see that same window opening there --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to mark it just -- because we can't see what you're pointing at.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm looking at - is the pen activated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can guess is that as the main prayer hall collapsed, it -- the domes also collapsed onto the next level down. But what I was trying to point out, and it's still not doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The pen doesn't seem to be functioning.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you see what I was trying to indicate there? Clearly there was a tremendous blast that was able to destroy the entire rear part of the building. You can see it from here. This is the side of the building. If we can go to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The photograph we were looking at is at the top of this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you could just scroll up, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is the pen not functioning? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, we can leave that, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- was I able to explain -- at the right-hand side of the arcade from the interior you can see that the walls come up and there is a very characteristic window there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The difficulty we have is the apparent disappearance of one whole level of the building with the domes relatively intact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- Your Honours, if I can draw upon my experience of looking at literally several hundred of such mosques that were destroyed by explosions, these modern mosque structures are made of elements of reinforced concrete. The little domes are constructed separately and then placed on top. They are not an integral part of the structure. In one case in Bosnia I saw such a mosque that had been blown up where the entire roof fell down on one side from two-storey height and the domes were still intact and the only wall still standing was the back of the mosque. So it is quite possible to drop these domes one storey without them disintegrating. There are only a few standard designs that these villages use, and to some extent these are prefabricated mosques, the arcades, and so forth. The main structure is just the same way that local houses are built nowadays, which is a concrete framework filled in with hollow brick.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we maybe see page 1 again of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in your view this photograph would have been taken - because we see the three domes are there - would have been taken from which angle?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be taken from the former interior looking towards the entrance. And you can see part of the base of the main dome folded down, that semicircle. The main dome originally rested upon a square base, and the square base has been blown out. And what remained of it has essentially folded down. So what looks like a vertical element in this picture was originally horizontal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the database entry that we saw earlier, this is 01778. I don't know if Your Honours have further questions on this specific set of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think as much as he can the witness has helped us. There's clearly lingering questions which we will have to study. This will be received, the database.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01133.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could look at a further photograph, this is 01801.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a photograph we just saw on the entry that we were looking at earlier for this mosque. If you could assist and indicate from which angle this photograph would have been taken. It's just an enlarged version from the one contained in the database entry.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my sense is that what we're looking at is the right-hand side -- if you were facing the entry, this would be taken from the right-hand side of the mosque. You see the collapsed main prayer hall at the right, and you see the folded-down base of the dome, and then you see the three domes collapsed onto the front structure there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to tender this photograph as 01801.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01134.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now move to 01787.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is one of the last sites that I would like to ask your comments on. This is again an entry from your database for the site of Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it's not the original colour one, so it's less readable, the photograph, but it's first of all not a site we visited; however, we had photograph from Mr. Bajgora and there was also an entry in the EU/IMG database. And as the entry indicates, the mosque was completely burned out. Only the perimeter walls remain. And there seemed to be large gaps in the wall, indicating that there were blown away by projectiles. In addition to the photos and the EU/IMG database, there was also a first-hand media report by a foreign reporter who was present in Ivaja which describes the damage to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit as 01787. We will search in our system to see if we have the colour copy, in which case we may apply at a later stage to replace this version with a colour copy just so we have a more readable version of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01135.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The last set of photographs I want to look at is 01789.01 and if we could look at page 7 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the interior of the Bayrakli mosque, or Mosque of Sultan Muhammad the Conquerer, in the centre of the city of Pec. Do you wish me to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're standing in the interior looking out through the entrance door on the left. What you're looking at is the remains of the women's balcony which was over the entrance. The wooden elements of the balcony have been completely burned, and there was intense heat inside the mosque. You can see at the ground level everything is charred. The marble columns have exploded from the heat. If you -- marble often has residual water in it, fossil water, and when exposed to very high heat, two things happen to marble: First of all the water expands and explodes, that you can see in the middle column, for example. And the other thing that can happen is, if the heat is high enough, marble is metamorphic limestone, and when you burn limestone you get cement. And the surface of these columns and of the marble cladding at the lower level of the mosque had been exposed to high enough heat that to a certain depth it had turned into powdery limestone. What was remarkable is that at higher levels of the mosque, the wall paintings were still intact, the roof, the walls were completely intact. And in fact, the large oaken entrance door was charred but still intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this a site you visited?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a site we visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we go to --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we go to -- October 1998? Is that the correct --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, October 1999. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could go to page 8, which is the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a mosque also in the city of Pec known in Albanian as Xhamia e Kuqe, that's K-u-q-e, or red mosque. It was one of several mosques in the city of Pec that had been burned out. What you can see from this photo which I took is, first of all, that the roof is missing, that there has been intense fire. And you can also tell that this is a mosque that has been set on fire from the inside and then burned because the entire floor of it is carpeted with an even, undisturbed carpet of roof tiles, broken only by the straight lines of the collapsed charred roof timbers. If it had been hit by any kind of projectile, you would have expected some disturbance, destruction of the roof or destruction of the walls.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now look at the next page of this exhibit. This is the last photograph I want to show you today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photo taken in the city of Pristina next to the Emperor's mosque in Pristina. What it shows is the historical archive of the Islamic Community of Kosovo on fire. The photo was taken on 13th June, 1999, by Oleg Popov, who is a photographer for Reuters. We bought the photo from the news agency. During our visit to Pristina in October of 1999, we visited the burned-out building and made an inspection of it. The building contained the historical archives of the Islamic Community, including the records of its properties and charitable endowments as well as several safes that had been broken open which, according to the Islamic Community spokesman we talked to, actually, Mr. Xhabir Hamiti, had contained the collections of charity money for the Bajram, for the major Muslim holiday. And according to Mr. Hamiti and of course also according to media reports that were published at the time it was burnt, the archive was burnt by Serb policemen just before the arrival of the first KFOR troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how do you know that? Where did you obtain this information that the archive had been burned by Serb policemen before the arrival of the first KFOR troops?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the two sources were, number one, the secretary of the Islamic Community said as much; and number two, there were several news reports by reporters who were present in Pristina at the time who gave the same account.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. There is -- this is a -- contains additional photographs which I haven't shown to the witness; however, they are -- they have been discussed in his previous testimony which is in evidence, and for reference this exhibit in the Milutinovic case was D1789. So I would seek to tender the entire set of photographs, although I have in the interests of saving time not gone through each one of them. And in this case this is 65 ter 01789.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01136.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And one final exhibit is 01791.01, if we could have that up on the screen. While that is being brought up, I was just informed by Ms. Pedersen that we do have a colour copy of Exhibit P1135, this is 65 ter 01787, which is -- relates to the mosque in Ivaja that we just saw five minutes ago. So I would ask with your leave to replace the version in e-court with a colour copy just because the quality of the photograph is better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, this is the final exhibit I would like to show you if you could just explain what this is.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an entry from the EU/IMG database. If you scroll up slightly -- I guess it doesn't have their letter-head above, it may have it below -- oh, yes, International Management Group, and they give the date when they did their assessment, in this case at the beginning of October of 1999. Each entry contains a photograph. It has the dimensions of the building and other technical data, and then in this case the damage valuation for the mosque itself is "totally destroyed," so they give no details. But you will note the various categories where they mention that it has no telephone link, no power-supply, and so forth. You can see a slightly better example down below for what they call building number 2 of the complex, which I assume must be the imam's house. Their damage categories are, walls and floors, roof, doors, and windows, interiors, and it seems to be a very complex calculus because the total has to be -- add up to 100, so in this case 7 per cent of the interior doesn't mean that it's -- 7 per cent of the interior got burned, but whatever the standard percentage is for the interior, it is that portion of it. You will also note that in categories where the mosque was not totally destroyed they would use the same assessment scale for a mosque, which makes it rather difficult to talk about a building, for example, which has lost the minaret. Where would you classify the minaret in those categories? So it has somewhat limited applicability. And I also noticed that if you go through all of the EU/IMG database there seem to have been slightly different readings of the categorisation in different municipalities, where in one municipality a building that was completely burned out and was missing its roof would be assigned a lower number than damage that looked almost identical in another municipality. Of course, it's sometimes very hard to tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would this be the type of entry that you looked at when you were preparing your report --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- and that you have cited in your own entries of your database?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. So in these EU/IMG entries, the most useful part of them for us was the photograph and the assessment was largely based on the photograph to the extent that we looked at their damage evaluation; there was some indication, as you saw in the case of Lastica, of interior or exterior damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01137.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I just need some time to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Riedlmayer. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, counsel for the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. Given the delicacy of your work, I feel it incumbent upon me to ask you questions that I hope will provide us with a greater insight on what you discussed today and on matters contained in your report to this Tribunal. Pursuant to that, first of all, I will have to ask you about your expertise. What is your academic title, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have a bachelor's degree in history, I have a master's degree in Near Eastern Studies, I have a degree in library and information science, and I'm a doctoral candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please be so kind to tell us this. You said that you have a degree in history. Could you please tell me whether this degree concerns a certain period in history or is it a general history degree.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My specialty was in Ottoman history, with a minor in Byzantine studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, where did you obtain this degree while you studied, which is -- that which is related to your specialty, the Ottoman history, that is in other words a part of the history of Turkey; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the first part of your question, I obtained my training in Ottoman history at the University of Chicago and at Princeton University. And the second observation I would make that it's not just part of the history of Turkey anymore than Habsburg history would be nearly the history of Austria. It is also part of the history of the Balkans and of the broader region that was part of the Ottoman Empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I focused only on the Ottoman history that you say you specialised in and that you are an expert in. I did not ask you anything about Habsburgs, I did not want to hear any comment about them, but anyway thank you. You said that you had a minor concerning Byzantine culture. What does it relate to, where did you obtain this degree, and could you be more specific in terms of what you graduated from in terms of Byzantine history?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. In the American educational system you get a -- in your bachelor's degree you get to choose a major and a minor field in which you take your examinations and your courses. I studied Byzantine history at the University of Chicago. I studied with Professor Speros Vryonis, with Professor Walter Kaegi, I took several courses in the history and culture of the Byzantine Empire. It seemed to be a useful supplement to the Ottoman history which, after all, temporally and in terms of geographic area, followed it. And it was also something that fit into my prior education since I had pursued a classical course in my pre-university education, so I had Latin and Greek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it fits part of your statement where you say that the Balkans has been a focus of your interest for the past 40 years or even more because that statement dates back a certain number of years. Would we agree on that, that this is the focus of your interest, the history of the Balkans as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said history. Now you've cleared it up. And then you mentioned Near East studies. How complementary that is for your degree in history. What about the other field, this other degree concerning Near Eastern Studies, what does it stand for? Of course in the context of the US educational system you can expound a bit more on that in replying to my question, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glad to. At Princeton University, where I had my graduate training, Ottoman history was part of the Department of Near Eastern Studies. Rather than be part of the History department. Within the Department of Near Eastern Studies, we were required to take courses not only in history as such but also in philology and in cultural history. So at Princeton I studied Ottoman Turkish, Arabic, Persian, as well as Ottoman historical sources and their readings and interpretations. That it was called Near Eastern Studies was merely the administrative arrangement at that particular university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I must, I'm afraid, interrupt, as I indicated yesterday and have reminded counsel. We must break early and at this time because of another commitment that I have, and we must have a longer-than-usual break. I'm sorry about this, sir, but there are other pressing matters. We expect to be able to resume in 40 minutes' time, at ten minutes to 1.00. Again, a Court Officer will assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I apologise, I was delayed longer than expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, we are going to continue where we stopped before the break. You were explaining what Near Eastern Studies meant at Princeton University. Now I'm interested in the latter part of your answer. Your library sciences training and education, when, where, and what does this mean, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my degree in -- another master's degree in library and information science at the Graduate School for Library and Information Science in Simmons College in Boston. I received my degree in 1988, although I had been pursuing it since the early 1980s. This is with a view to specialisation in art documentation, which concerns the documentation of works of art and the systemisation of the information about works of art. Since 1985 I have directed the Document Centre for Islamic Art and Architecture at Harvard and as part of that position I've also pursued continuing education in taking courses on artistry and also attending conferences on art documentation. I don't know if that answers your question, art history.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm interested in is whether your work in this field was directed not only at culture of the Islamic Community, but whether your interests went beyond culture and art or were you just limited to Islamic culture and tradition which is connected to culture and arts?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The answer to your question is, first of all, the work I've done concerns every culture that had contact with Islamic culture. So it includes not only the cultural production of Islamic communities, but also the cultural production of communities that were in contact with Islam. Secondly, as the director of an art documentation centre, in addition to dealing with works of art as such, I also have an interest in related fields such as art law which deals with the regulation of the trade in art and artefacts. And in the late 1980s and early 1990s I developed a project to work up a source book on the legal protection of cultural property with a special focus on the Middle East. This was an outgrowth of the First Gulf War. And I even had a publisher who -- that was interested, but then events overtook that and that project never came to fruition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, do you still work as a bibliographer within the Aga Khan Program on Islamic culture at the Harvard University Library?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my official title.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to explain briefly what stands behind the Aga Khan Program, who founded it, how it is funded, and what does its existence mean within the context of the Harvard University. This would be my first question but contains a number of subordinate questions. I believe you'll be able to manage it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best. First of all, the Aga Khan Program for Islamic architecture was set up in 1979 as a joint programme between Harvard University and Massachusetts Institute of Technology, MIT, and it was established by a donation from His Highness Karim Aga Khan. Karim Aga Khan is one of the many wealthy graduates of Harvard University. He received his degree from Harvard in 1961. And since he got his degree, like many Harvard graduates, he was persuaded to give a donation to the university. In his case he established a chair in Islamic art history and the documentation centre was part of the donation for the chair. The way such things work at American universities is once an endowment is made the university manages the endowment and the income of the endowment supports the activities of the endowment. So in this case the activities support the Aga Khan professor at various conferences, the activities of the documentation centre, fellowships and scholarships for students and visiting scholars, and so forth. The Aga Khan, as you may know, is the head of the Ismaili Shia Community which is a sect of Islam and he has both inherited wealth and wealth that comes to him through donations of his community, while he takes an active interest in various cultural enterprises of his own through the Aga Khan Foundation, the Aga Khan Award for Architecture, and other enterprises. The programme at Harvard subsists independently for the past 25 years as part of Harvard University, so he doesn't direct what happens in the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was an exhaustive answer, and I hope that we will draw many conclusions from it. The next thing I'm interested in is as follows. The programme and the main objectives of the Aga Khan Foundation or endowment of the library which contains many documents headed by you as far as I could gather, what are those main objectives of the Aga Khan endowment and this library and programme?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main objectives are to support research and teaching in the fields of Islamic architecture, Islamic art history, and archaeology. We support both the faculty and the students as well as researchers who come to us from every part of the world. And we also have publications that we issue. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Question to the interpreters: Do you want me to switch off my mike? I would like to ask the Court for this question to me from the interpreters to be sorted out through their technicians because this is going to be very vexing for me to switch on and switch off my microphone. There was no noise ensuing from that, and this will disturb me if I have to switch it on and off during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Normal practice which other counsel follow, Mr. Djordjevic, is to switch on and off. So we would ask you to follow that practice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I have not been doing so for the past six months. I will try to do so, but I have to admit that this affects my concentration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my next question concerning the Aga Khan Program - and this is going to be the last one concerning the Aga Khan Program - is as follows: You said that Karim Aga Khan is the head of an important significant Shia religious community of the Muslims. Does this mean that the Aga Khan Program deals with the culture of other Muslim communities, Sunni Muslims and others? Or is it focused strictly to the Shia Muslim community. As far as I recall you referred to that community.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a sectarian programme. It is an academic programme that looks at Islamic culture in the broadest sense, including, as I mentioned before, the interactions between Islamic culture and non-Muslim cultures. What it does focus on is the visual aspects of this culture, so the visual arts, architecture, arts of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but in any case I did not want to use this word "sectarian" or a "sect" when referring to Shia Muslims. This is a significant traditional community. Maybe you've misunderstood my drift. I will have no further questions concerning this. My next topic is your associate, the architect, Herscher. Would you please tell us what you know about his academic background -- sorry, I apologise. First of all, you said that you are preparing your doctoral thesis. Let's wrap-up this thing. Could you please tell us the title and the subject matter of your doctoral thesis and at which university.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I did not say I'm preparing my doctoral thesis. I said I was admitted to candidacy. That was at Princeton University. I went and did some thesis research and then decided not to pursue a thesis. So I remain a candidate, as having passed by exams, but I decided not to pursue that career. Now, can we go on to Mr. Herscher or would you like to ask other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. This is sufficient. Now let's please address the question about Mr. Herscher that I put to you a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Andrew Herscher, who prepared this report along with me, is a trained architect. And at the time I got to know him he was in the final stages of his doctoral work in architectural history, theory, and criticism at Harvard University. He worked in his master's thesis, he worked on Slovenian architecture. He also had some involvement in the post-war conservation of architecture in Mostar, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And most importantly for -- aside from his architectural qualifications, he also had some acquaintance with the languages and cultures of the region. After we finished our survey work, Mr. Herscher went on to work for the culture sector of the United Nations Mission in Kosovo, first as assistant head of the department of culture and then eventually as the head of the department of culture within UNMIK. He completed his doctorate in 2002 and he currently teaches as a professor of architecture at the University of Michigan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's revisit line 4, page 40 [as interpreted]. It says here: [In English] "... worked on Slovenian architecture." [Interpretation] I believe that this is an honest mistake. It is supposed to be Slavic architecture, not Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it Slovenian --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did his work on a Slovenian architect, whose name escapes me at the moment, a very famous man who designed the National Library in Ljubljana in the 1930s. And his doctoral work had to do with Czech architecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is clearer now. Could you please expound on him knowing the Balkan languages. Could you please shed some more light on that.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his linguistic expertise, such as it was, was due to the fact that he had studied and worked in Prague, so he was -- had some fluency in Czech. He had also lived in Ljubljana and knew Slovenian. And he had spent some time in Bosnia and by extrapolation he picked up some Serbo-Croatian. What this meant for our practical purposes is that he had enough knowledge of Serbo-Croatian that he could read some of the published documentation that came from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to what you worked on, did you study art history?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. My degree is not in art history, but I have taken many courses in art history, both in my undergraduate career and in my continuing education in the 25 years that I've worked at Harvard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: During your studies, did you have any contact with technical sciences, with civil engineering and architecture?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not an engineer and I'm not an architect. The fact that Mr. Herscher came with me was thereby an enhancement to our team because he brought an expertise that I could not claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware that you are not an architect or a civil engineer. All I wanted to know is if there were any subjects or courses during university that had some points in common with these two subjects, but anyway. My next question is: If before 1999 you worked on a similar project, photographing the damage of cultural monuments in any country in the similar way that you worked in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have experience in photo documentation of architecture, both in carrying it out first-hand and in analysing it and using it to put together databases, but certainly nothing comparable to the field-work I did in Kosovo in the sense that none of these projects concerned a post-war situation as such. But yes, I have gone on photo-documentation expeditions and also evaluated the work of others who have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us if you worked on similar jobs in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Either one.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I did carry out a survey in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the summer of 2001 under the auspices of the Tribunal, on a contract from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you just --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- tell me briefly -- can you just, please, tell me briefly what was the nature of this contract and exactly what did you do for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given terms of reference to look into documenting the wartime damage to the cultural and religious heritage of the non-Serb communities in a number of Bosnian municipalities. The methodology I pursued was very similar to that of the Kosovo survey, except that it was not extended over the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina but was limited -- more limited in scope. And also, unlike in the case of Kosovo where I documented every community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was limited to the non-Serb communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you would agree with me if we were to note that the Serbian community was not part of your work in the project that you did in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct. The terms of reference for my mission, I believe mainly for reasons of economy, concentrated on the matters which had been charged in the indictment which this was supposed to assist the Court in dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, you've confused me a little bit now. What I understood was that you were assessing the damage of the cultural monuments of the non-Serb community in Yugoslavia without assessing the financial amount of the damage and the actual damage overall which was important. But can you please tell us what the main objective was, the assessment of cultural monuments, the extent of the damage, or did it have more to do with the economic aspect of your expert mission?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike the EU/IMG mission which was designed to provide a base-line of how much money would be needed to reconstruct the buildings. The survey that Mr. Herscher and I carried out in Kosovo and my subsequent surveys in Bosnia had to do with us simply establishing the damage. The categorisation of the buildings as to age and whether they had been listed monuments protected under law before the war served, especially in the case of Kosovo, for the purpose of establishing priorities for reconstruction. But we did not propose to do economic estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have clarified this matter as well. In your CV you refer, amongst other things - I'm talking about the latest updated CV from 2001 - that you were -- [In English] Department of culture United Nations Mission in Kosovo, UNMIK, conducting an assessment of the states of books in Serbian and other languages in the Mitrovica library. Can you explain to us your function during that period?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This occurred in April of 2001, I believe. I was already in Kosovo on my last return mission as part of our three-part survey. And while I was in Kosovo I was asked by the department of culture, without any remuneration, to carry out an assessment of books in the Mitrovica public library. There had been allegations made that Serbian books, books in the Serbian language, in the Mitrovica public library had been discarded or destroyed. And so I carried out the survey in conjunction with a member of the department of culture, Madam Sophie Massal, and spent a day assessing the contents of the library. We measured the shelf metres of books according to language, we looked at the condition of the books, and we came up with some conclusions. The report is available on various web sites, including that of UNESCO and of the International Federation of Library Associations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you please tell me whether the library is in the part of Kosovska Mitrovica on this part of the Ibar River, the northern side towards Serbia in the Serbian part of Mitrovica as they used to refer to it. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the library in question is on the south side of the Ibar River. It existed from the time when the town had not been divided. It's just south of the river. And after June of 1999, the Serbian director and staff departed to the north side of Mitrovica and eventually the Albanian municipality appointed a new director on the south side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is already on the next item on your CV where it says that from 1999 until 2006 you were the co-founder -- [In English] " ...of Kosovo Cultural Heritage Project and NGO formed to help restore cultural monuments in Kosovo damaged in the 1998 till 1999 war." Can you tell us about that time. What is your function and what was the problems that you deal with?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we originally conceived of the survey project, the project had to have a name. We called it the Kosovo Cultural Heritage Project. I will note that this was an independent undertaking between Mr. Herscher and myself, and we got our funding from outside the university. We did the survey in part to see what cultural heritage had been damaged and to help the new UN authorities to deal with means of mitigating that damage. Unfortunately, when the UN administration came in in Kosovo it was not well prepared. The United Nations had never had a civil administration mission before, and it took them almost a year to set up a department of culture. Meanwhile, Mr. Herscher and I were very concerned that nothing was being done to protect and to repair some of the important war-damaged monuments. So we went back to the Packard Foundation for a subvention for another donation to help repair war-damaged monuments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the Packard Foundation, we will deal with that a little later. Perhaps we can just stop here for now and stay on this project. From what we see here, we see that it was focused on providing assistance for the restoration of cultural monuments in Kosovo which were damaged in the 1998/1999 war. What I'm interested in is, as the co-founder and director of this project, did you actually manage to provide real, effective help and was there any restoration done when you were director and co-founder? Because I see that the project continues until 2006. Did you manage to secure any funds? What was restored of the cultural heritage and the monuments in Kosovo in that period? Who provided the funds? And so on. That would be the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. The short answer is: Yes. We did manage to do some hands-on projects. The first subvention came already in December of 1999. We got a small $10.000 donation from the Packard Foundation, roughly $10.000, to buy emergency plastic sheeting to put on damaged monuments so that they would survive the first winter of the war. The problem is when a building has been burnt out and the elements enter into it, the rubble gets saturated with water. It freezes and expands and causes further damage to the building. So UNHCR would not provide the plastic. We provided the plastic and gave it to the Institute for the Protection of Monuments in Kosovo which then distributed to a variety of sites. That was step one. Step two we proposed to the Packard Foundation, the same funding agency, an ambitions project of doing a group of monuments. We would do one damaged mosque, one damaged church, and at least one damaged work of civil architecture. The mosque project actually came to fruition, that was the Hadum mosque in Gjakova, and Packard funded the first stage of that conservation. It is now being continued under UNESCO. The negotiations over a church we had proposed, the church in Drsnik [Realtime transcript read in error "Rznic"], eventually broke down in our contacts with the Serbian Orthodox church authorities. They insisted that such work had to be done through the preservation authorities in Belgrade. The UN authorities were unhappy with us, and eventually there was no way of arriving at any solution. Eventually we found a partnership with the Swedish NGO, cultural heritage without borders, who used some of our funding for the civil architecture part. This included both some "kullas," traditional Albanian houses, in a number of places and also a "konak" in Velika Hoca. This was a residential building owned by the Serbian Orthodox Church. The church restorations, unfortunately, did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since there will probably be another trial continuing this afternoon, I'm going to put one more question and then we will continue tomorrow. I'm not clear which church you're talking about. The one in Rznic or I heard something else. Perhaps you corrected yourself, let's just clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church we had in mind was Drsnik, D-r-s-n-i-k.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you agree, I think that this is a convenient moment for us to stop for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. I'm afraid our time has run again. We must continue tomorrow at 9.00. So a Court Officer will assist you when we leave the bench, Mr. Riedlmayer, and we look forward to completing your evidence tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 17th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
